newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call money ends steady, gilt yields down.
newsitem.headline: Indian call money ends steady, gilt yields down.

text.p: Indian call money ended Friday around 10.9 percent in steady trade, dealers said.
They said there was little fluctuation in rates during the day with most of the trade done between 10.75 percent and 11.0 percent.
"Rates are unlikely to remain below 11 percent because of the availability of export refinance," said a dealer.
Banks can avail refinance from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) against their export credit disbursals at a rate of 11 percent per annum.
Dealers said prices of government securities firmed up in brisk trade as banks sought to build up positions ahead of a cash reserve ratio (CRR) cut on January 4.
The RBI announced on Thursday that banks' CRR would be cut by one percentage point to 10 percent, in two slabs of 50 basis points each on January 4 and January 18, 1997.
"Some market participants are buying bonds anticipating a fall in interest rates after the CRR cut," said a dealer. "This is pushing prices up and yields down."

The 13.50 percent 1998 government of India stock traded on Friday at a yield of 11.85 percent against its last traded 12.08 percent, dealers said. The 12 percent 1999 yielded 13.08 percent against 13.15 while the 13.5 percent 1997 was down to 10.85 percent from 11.85, they said.
No trades were reported in commercial paper or certificates of deposit.
